title: The Origin of the Word Arya

THE ORIGIN OF THE WORD 'ARYA'

BY

V. J. TAMBY PILLAI ESQ., M.R.A.S. (Ceylon)

THE name 'Aryas' () by which the Vedic race called itself in times of pre-historic antiquity seems to furnish a very important and interesting point of contact between that race and the primitive Dravidians. It is held to be a purely Sanscrit term derived from a primordial root akin to, or identical with, the Latin and Greek ar meaning 'to plough' and, hence, it has been inferred that, at first, it meant 'a cultivator', and then 'a lord' or 'a nobleman', which latter meaning it is said to retain till today. It may, however, be pointed out here that that eminent Sanscritist, the late Dr. K. M. Bannerjea of Calcutta, did not concur in the above explanation. He theorized that the word was originally of Semitic extraction but adopted into, and naturalized in, Sanscrit in later times. If the true history of the term and of its connexion with Sanscrit be that given by the learned Dr. Bannerjea, we need no further proof to show that the true 'Aryas' of antiquity were a race, not the same as that from which the primitive Sanscritians sprang. It is possibly a historical fact that the country beyond the Western frontier of the Punjab known as 'Ariana',*

* Bochart proves that Media was called Ara or Aria from Hara, a place where the Assyrian kings Pul and Tiglathpilesar had vanquished the Reuvenites, the Gadites and the half tribe of Manasseh (vide I Chronicles. chap : 5, v. 26). The name Ariyan appears thus to be of Semitic origin, but adopted and naturalized in Sanscrit.

'A Turanian invasion of Media, as was suggested by Dr. Oppert, was probably the cause of the introduction of the name Media and the as Dr. Bannerjea says, for some centuries preceding the Christian era, was anciently inhabited by the forefathers of the later Sanscrit-speaking races of Hindustan. This forms, however, no irrefragable proof of any primordial connexion between the primitive Sanscritians and the name of 'Aryas' now applied to them. For, there is nothing to preclude the supposition that the country might have been so named on account of its having been the residence of a pre-Semitic or Turanian race long before it came into the possession of the ancestors of the Indic Sanscritians. Moreover, if the conclusion of many an antiquarian may be relied on that the ancient Semites were indebted to their neighbours for most of their culture and arts, we are not, then, wrong in carrying the pedigree of the art of husbandry further back to the times when the Bels of Chaldea ruled supreme in the regions of the Persian Gulf. Referring

consequent expulsion of the Ariyans from their primitive home.' The Ariyan Witness by Rev. Dr. K. M. Bannerjea, pp. 83, 93 and 91.)

If 'Hara', or 'Ara' was, in fact, the primitive yocable from which the word 'Arya' was in subsequent times evolved, the suggestion may not be out of place that the Tamils with whom the Brahminical races are admitted to have freely mixed were known also by a name significantly corresponding to 'Hara' or 'Ara'—I mean the name 'Arava' by which they are called even to-day by their neighbours. It is here necessary to refute the following dictum born of prejudice of the author of The Indian Empire, viz. 'many words have been borrowed (by the Indo-Aryan vernaculars) from Dravidian languages generally in a contemptuous sense. Thus the common word pilla, "cub," is really a Dravidian word meaning "son"." (vide p: 363). The above observation is obviously based on incorrect information. 'Pillai' in Tamil means 'child' and not 'son' and is used to denote not only a human child but also the young of a parrot, a squirrel, a mungoose, a young cocoanut-palm a young areca-palm, &c., &c. There is no reason to doubt that 'pillai' was in ancient times used to signify not only a human child but also the young of all domesticated or pet animals of the Tamil people. To make the case stronger I would cite that of the word 'kulavi' (குலவி) which though now restricted in meaning to a human child was used also in ancient Tamil to connote the young of beasts. 'Kulavi' and 'pillai' are words meaning the same thing and their usages were most probably also similar. to the position of the pure Semites with regard to civilization, the great German savant, Dr. F. R. Grau of Konisburg says, 'If the idea of culture is understood in the sense in which the Hamites laid its foundations and the Indo-European erected thereon the magnificent structure of modern civilization, then the Semites as a whole must be excluded from the list of civilized nations. . . . For, while around them flourished various forms of Hamitic civilization, they were destitute of everything which could be compared with them; . . . (among them) no science, no art, was developed, no industry or even trade, sprang up.'* Is it probable, then, that the Aryans learnt the art of agriculture from the Semitic nomads? To quote Dr. Grau once more, 'Mankind owes to the Hamites the first great development of agriculture. It was not merely to the fertility of the low lands that their agricultural success was due, but rather to their rational system of management. An agricultural literature sprang up among the ancient Hamites, also at a very early period.'†

The improbability, then, of a term meaning 'cultivator' first originating among a race of shepherds such as the Semites are known to have been, when they emerge in history, is a strong proof of its non-Semitic derivation. In so far as its relation to the dialect of the Vedic race is concerned, the following lines would seem to contain all that has hitherto been said about it by those who have believed in its Sanscritian origin, viz. the term 'Arya' in modern Sanscrit means 'noble,' or 'of good family', and it is probably connected with the root 'ar' which, in both Greek and Latin, means 'to plough' and which appears in English in the word 'ear-th' meaning literally 'what is ploughed' from an old English word 'to ear' meaning 'to plough'. The Aryas. perhaps, it is further explained, used this word to distinguish themselves as an agricultural nation with a settled home from the wandering tribes of Tartars that surrounded them.

It need hardly be pointed out that this theory is, at best, a mere conjecture as no satisfactory proof has yet been added to show that 'Arya' ever meant, in primitive Sanscrit, 'a husbandman', or that agriculture was, at any time, regarded by the primitive Sanscritians as a noble occupation. For while 'the Hamites settled in fruitful and alluvial plains' well-suited for agriculture, 'the Indo-Europeans preferred mountains and heights unfavourable for developing the first germs of civilization.' 'The primitive Indo-European nation was, probably, still in that peculiar state of transition in which agriculture is only temporarily carried on and is subordinated to cattle breeding as it is now the case among many Arab tribes.'*

It will thus be seen that the great agricultural races of the ancient world were necessarily of the Hamitic or Cushite stock, and that, if the primitive Sanscritians were ever indebted to any race for their knowledge of systematic husbandry, these must have been a Cushite people and not Semites. Further, no trace of the supposed pre-eminence of the agricultural class amongst the primitive Sanscrit-speaking tribes can be shown to exist in their language or writings, and this fact, considering the great amount of old literature in Sanscrit that has come down to our day, seems fatal to any supposition or inference that the term 'Arya' was primarily the tribal name of the agricultural fore-fathers of the Sanscritic Indians. Are we able to glean any evidence from Sanscrit literature that the cultivating classes at any time held the highest rank in the social arrangements of the ancient Sanscritians? The answer to this question is neither difficult nor far to seek. In their social and political organization, it was the priest who, it is commonly believed, held the foremost place, while, the cultivator was, in point of rank or precedence, considered lower than even the rude swordsman who often led the life of a free-booter or marauder.* The impossibility of deriving an honoured name from that of a despised class is too evident to be mistaken and unless it can be proved that the mass of literature in Sanscrit presents things in a way quite the reverse of what they actually were in times of old, the suggestion that the 'Aryas' were, at first, a race of farmers must be abandoned as utterly groundless. Sir M. M. William, in his Indian Wisdom, says, 'the very name Arya is, as every one now knows, connected with the root ri=ar, whence aratrum, 'a plough,' (e.g. Sanscrit aritra). It is curious to note how the Brahmans, after their segregation as the dominant class, sought to deprecate agriculture. Manu (X. 84) says: 'Some think that agriculture (krishi) is an excellent thing, but it is a mode of existence blamed by the good, because the iron-mouthed plough-share wounds the earth and the creatures living in it.' To this, the author of The Vedic India, which may be said to be a summary, in many important respects, of the conclusions and inferences arrived at by a large number of Indo-logists of European reputation, replies as follows, viz: 'it has been suggested — but the attractive suggestion has unfortunately not proved capable of sufficient scientific proof — that the name "Arya" itself is connected with this root (e.g. ar= to plough,) and the people who took it for their own originally meant to call themselves "the people who plough" in proud distinction from their sheep-raising, steppe-roaming, the robber neighbours, the Turanians. But, at the time at which we begin to know them Arya meant noble, exalted, venerable.* It is well known to students of history that 'upon the fall of Carthage, the Romans handed over to their African allies the libraries of their fallen foes, retaining, however, the great work of Mago, a contemporary of Cyrus, on agriculture which consisted of twenty-eight volumes, and dealt with all branches of the art. It was, subsequently, at the request of the Senate, translated into Latin. But, Carthage, in this as in other branches of culture, was merely the missionary and intermediary of the Babylonians and the Egyptians. The existence of the book of Nabathaean agriculture proves beyond doubt that the art of husbandry was highly developed in ancient Chaldea while there exists positive monumental evidence of the times of "The Ancient Empire" of Egypt that it was then in a state of high development in that country.'† In the opinion of the famous Liebig, modern people can rival the Mongolian Chinese in their rational method of agriculture, while Sir John Hewett, in his treatise on The Pre-historic Ruling Races says that the Dravidians were, of all the great races of antiquity, the first to systematize agriculture.

The Rig-Veda is supposed to be a very ancient book. Some scholars have even ascribed to certain hymns of its earlier chapters an antiquity far higher than the time of the entrance of the ancestors of the Sanscritic Indians into the land of the Five Rivers—an antiquity co-eval with the times when the remote ancestors of the Vedic Rishis lived in peace and comfort in their primordial habit at near the North Pole offering sacrifices and singing hymns to their god or gods or powers of nature.‡ Now, the word 'Arya' frequently occurs in the hymns of the Rig, and if its composition really dates in that far-off age of the past when the common progenitors of the Sanscritic Indians, the Greeks, the Latins, the Schlaves, the Kelts, and the Teutons yet lived together in regions outside the boundaries of India, it follows that the use of the appellation 'Arya' must have been equally current among the early European races belonging to these nationalities as among those whose descendants called themselves by that name on the plains of Hindustan. But, strangely enough, not one of these European races who, by the affiliation of language, have been proved to belong to the same ethnological stock with the Sanscritic Indians now remembers, or have preserved even, the slightest trace of the fact of their being once known by the name of 'Aryas'; and this is even still more strange and inexplicable in the case of the Hellenistic and the Latin races, as it seems most probable that if the term did actually exist in the old common mother tongue of the Indo-Aryan group of races, it would have found a place in the rich vocabulary of ancient Greece which possessed a literature reaching far back, it is said, into

'the five tribes—Yadus, Duruvasus, Duruhyus, Anus and Purus', 'the worshippers of Indra' &c., &c., &c. Besides 'Yadus and Duruvasus', says Mr. Lewis Rice, 'Yayati had three sons, Drahyu, Anu and Puru and the collective people of the five races who claimed to be descended from these were the Dravidian Bharatas under Visvamitra who resisted the Aryan advance under Vashishta.' (Vide The Gazetter of Mysore by Lewis Rice M.A., Chap: on Ethnology.')

The author of the Vedic India writing almost in the same strain says that the Baharatas and the Purus were originally Dravidians. (Vedic India, pp. 328, 319, 324). Add to the above the tradition that the progenitor Manu who with seven others survived the deluge was, according to the Puranas in which are preserved undoubtedly the traditions and myths of pre-historic Bharathavarsha, a king of the Dravida country of the race of the Pandyas. It may be noted also that Yadu and Duruvasu, whom the Puranas, the Tamil liturature and South Indian inscriptions connect with the Dravidians, are always mentioned together in the Rig Veda and lived in the regions of the Yamuna on the banks of which the ancient Madura is said to have been rounded by the ancestors of the Pandyas. antiquity. This applies as well to the Latin language which is equally guiltless of possessing any evidence that the term 'Arya' was a household name of the primitive Romans. Some have ventured by artificial and fanciful derivations and explanations to connect terms which, in form, are utterly unlike one other. As an instance of these feats of philology, I would just repeat* what Mr. Kunte, who was a staunch believer in the common origin of the Sanscritic Hindus, and the old Greeks and the Teutons of Europe, has stated on this point. He says 'Arya', when it is pronounced, as a Londoner pronounces 'arm' into 'harm', becomes 'harya', and being slightly modified, it passed into 'Hellas' the name of the Hellas. 'Hellaspont' i.e. Ariapatha was so named on account of its being the highway of the 'Aryas'. The Germans converted the 'Harya' into 'Herr' which has passed into 'Sir' of the English language. Some insignificant tribes pressed from behind by stronger Aryas, penetrated into Italy, and settled in its different parts husbanding their energy, but occupying the fertile portions of the peninsula under different names. Hence, there is no name in Latin that exactly corresponds to 'Arya' in sound, or sense.† And likewise, the ancient Schalves also had no remembrance of their once being 'Aryas.' These are opinions, which, in view of the great names that support them, cannot, I admit, be despised. It may, however, be observed that if the evolution of the 'Aryapatha' of the Brahmans into the 'Hellespont' of the Greeks be a fact, the day cannot be far distant when we shall be told to believe that the 'Ravaneswara' of the South Indian Kurumbas is only an evolved form of the 'Unkulun-Kulu' of the South African Zulus.

Having been so far concerned with the term 'Arya' in its Sanscritic relations, we shall now proceed to enquire if it is possible to connect it with any Dravidian source. It is now generally admitted that the Vedic Sanscritians were not at all a pure race, their ancestors having freely intermarried with the pre-Aryan tribes who opposed their advance into the plains of the Ganges. It was pointed out years ago by Dr. Taylor that a Tamiloid language, now represented by its most cultivated branch in the South, constituted the original staple of all the languages of India. The existence of a Tamilian substratum in all the modern dialects of India and of the profound influence which the classical Tamil has exercised on the formation and development of both the Vedic and the classical Sanscrit, is gradually coming to be recognized by students of Indian philology. Further, modern investigations have shown that the bulk of the population of Northern India, so far as their racial affinities are concerned, contain a common factor essentially Dravidian in blood. Says an eminent authority: 'From an ethnological point of view, the Aryans of India are not a pure race as they appear to have been when they dwelt in the valley of the Indus; for, in the Veda, a contrast is often drawn between a clear complexion and the dark skin of the indigenous people. They must, on the contrary, have mixed with the natives at some period when a peculiar civilization was in development, and not only has the physical type greatly altered its original Indo-European character, but the whole civilization of the Indians has received the stamp of Southern and Eastern Asia which makes them appear to us even stranger than the Asiatic Semites or the Egyptians. This fact is often overlooked, because the use of the Aryan speech continually reminds us of the close relationship between the Indian Aryans and the Persians and Europeans; and it is not merely that the Aryans have assumed the racial marks of the Dravidians, but, on the other hand, the pure type of the indigenous population has only been preserved in the uncivilized mountain peoples.* If in this mixture of the races and the languages of ancient India, we see the origin of a Sanscritic Dravidian race in the north of India, many centuries anterior to our era, it becomes easy to explain how the Tamil term 'Aryan' came to be adopted into the primitive Sanscrit. It is also by no means improbable that the primitive abodes of the two races were in contiguous regions, and that the process of miscegenation had already been in progress when they started on their journey towards the frontiers of the Punjab. Again, the literature, traditions and the customs of the Tamilians support the pre-eminent respectability of the calling of husbandry and hence it is that the social distinctions observed among them have been essentially different from those prevailing among the races of Northern India.

To the Dravidian, there was, indeed, nothing nobler than the yoke and the plough which were to him the very emblems of freedom, honour and virtue. In his estimation, he only was a real freeman to whom the plough was the sole means of livelihood, while all others were, in fact, only servants. That a word once meaning 'a farmer' among such people should have, in the course of time, come to signify 'a noble person' would, therefore, seem to be nothing difficult to appreciate.* It is remarkable that the Tamil êt (çî) assumes the form âr (çî) in Kanarese from which ûriyar (çflwî) in the sense of 'cultivators' is easily derived. The Hala (Old) Kannada in which the older literature of the Kornatas is written preserves, undoubtedly, many primitive forms and expressions of the parent-tongue of the Tamilians, and the Kanarese âr (çî) represents, possibly, the more ancient form of the word.

If it be contended, however, that 'Arya' really meant in Sanscrit not 'husbandman' but 'a noble person,' it is hardly more necessary than to invite attention to the detailed discussion of this point in an earlier issue of this journal† in which an endeavour was made to prove that 'Aryan' (çflwç) meaning 'a great or exalted person' is Tamil in origin. If one only keeps in view the fact that Tamil is by far older‡ than Sanscrit, and that the latter even in its earlier

* 'Amongst the pure Tamils the class most honoured was that of the Arivar or 'sages.' Arivar were ascetics: but of the men living in society the farmers occupy the highest position. They formed the nobility or the landed aristocracy of the country. They are now known as Mudalis or 'the first caste.', (The Tamils Eighteen Hundred Years Ago, pp. 113-4.)

'Their (the Tamils') civilization was certainly older than that of the Aryas, for amongst the latter the fighting men were next in rank to the priests, whereas among the Tamils the farmers were next to the religious men, the military class was below even that of the herdsmen and artisans. . . To this day the Vellala does not take meals or drink water at the house of a Padaiyatchi, who calls himself a Kshatriya or a merchant who passes for a Vaisya' (Vide ibidem, p. 116.)

† The Tamilian Antiquary No. I, pp. 45-9. (2nd Edition, pp. 42-3.)

‡ It (Tamil) stands alone without any immediate predecessor. In origin it must be long anterior to the Sanscrit. Professor Rhys Davids, in his Buddhistic India, commenting on the evolution of the Aryan languages of India, maintains that the Vedic Sanscrit is largely mixed up with the primitive Dravidian.

There is little doubt that the Dravidian languages are incomparably older in point of time than Sanscrit. It is not an unreasonable supposition that they once occupied the whole of Hindustan and have been driven to stages of growth contained a large admixture of the primitive Dravidian, the strangeness of the phenomenon of the Aryo-Dravidian* or Vedic race of old calling itself by a name indigenous to India must, in a large measure, disappear.

their present position to the South and along the coast by the encroachment of other languages coming from the north-west. (Vide, The Manual of the Administration of the Madras Presidency, by Dr. Maclean, pp. 42, 112-3).

* 'We may assume for our present purpose that the ancestors of the Indo-Aryans came into India from the north-west and that at the time of their arrival the Peninsula, as far as the valley of the Ganges and the Jumna, was in the possession of the Dravidians. . . For the origin of the Aryo-Dravidian type we need not travel beyond the ingenious hypothesis put forward by Dr. Hoernle twenty years ago and confirmed by the recent researches of Dr. Grierson's Linguistic Survey. This theory supposes that after the first swarm of Indo-Aryans had occupied the Punjab, a second wave of Aryan-speaking people, the remote ancestors of the Aryo-Dravidians of to-day, . . made their way into India through Gilget and Chitral and established themselves in the plains of the Ganges and Jumna the sacred middle-land (Madhyadesa) of post-Vedic tradition. Here they came in contact with the Dravidians; . . here the Vedas were composed and the whole fantastic structure of orthodox ritual and usage was built up. The linguistic evidence in favour of this view is summarized in Dr. Grierson's chapter on Language in the Report on the Census of India, 1901. For the present purpose it is sufficient to note that the record of physical characters bears out the conclusions suggested by philology. The type of the people now dwelling in the middle-land is precisely what might have been expected to result from the incursion of a fair, long-headed race travelling by a route which prevented women from accompanying them, into a land inhabited by dark-skinned Dravidians. The men of the stronger race took to themselves the women of the weaker, and from these unions was evolved the mixed type which we find in Hindustan and Bihar.

'It (this theory) explains how it is that the Vedic Hymns contain no reference to the route by which the Aryans entered India or to their earlier settlement on the Indus; and it accounts for the antagonism between the eastern and the western sections and for the fact that the latter were regarded as comparative barbarians by the more cultured inhabitants of the middle-land.' (Vide Imperial Gazetteer of India. The Indian Empire, Vol. I, New Edition, pp. 300, 303-4.)

This king raised the Mahisyas, it is said, over the Banias thus changing the social usages of old Bengal in conformity with the practices of the Tamils.

At Rogozin 'for thousand in our languages or more correctly in the parent languages of ours—Sanscrit, Greek, Latin', Old Teutonic having each fabricated a word of its own . . . as to our Aryan forefather, we cannot escape the inference from this fact that they could count only up to a hundred-the numerals so far coinciding in all Aryan languages with almost comical regularity; . . . they may have known of thousands as so many 'tens of hundreds,' and counted . . . twelve hundred, eighteen hundred and so on.' The Vedic India p. 73. The above seems to be a conclusive proof of the Sanscrit 'Sahasra' being a modified form of the Tamil 'Aiyiram' 'thousand' the intermediate steps being 'Sayiram, Sasiram, and Sahasiram.
